def: The scientific study of mind and behaviour, covering everything from nerve cells to whole societies.
The long-standing philosophical question of how mental experience relates to the physical body and brain.
The view, associated with René Descartes, that mind and body are fundamentally different kinds of substance that interact.
The position that knowledge comes mainly from sensory experience and observation rather than from inborn ideas.
The view that some knowledge, abilities or mental structures are inborn rather than acquired through experience.
The question of how much behaviour and mental traits arise from heredity versus environment; modern work stresses that the two constantly interact.
An early school, linked to Wundt and Titchener, that tried to break conscious experience down into its basic elements using trained introspection.
A method in which trained observers carefully report on their own conscious experience in response to controlled stimuli.
Wundt's approach stressing that the mind actively organises and directs its elements through will and attention.
A school, associated with William James, that asked what mental processes are for and how they help organisms adapt to their environment.
A German school arguing that perception is organised into wholes that are more than the sum of their parts.
Freud's theory and therapy holding that unconscious conflicts, often rooted in childhood, shape thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
In psychodynamic theory, mental content and processes that influence behaviour but lie outside awareness.
A psychoanalytic technique in which the client says whatever comes to mind without censoring it, to reveal hidden material.
An approach, championed by Watson and Skinner, that limited psychology to observable behaviour and its environmental causes.
A perspective, led by Maslow and Rogers, emphasising free will, personal growth and each person's potential for self-actualisation.
The mid-20th-century shift back toward studying internal mental processes such as memory and reasoning, helped by computing and linguistics.
The study of mental processes such as attention, memory, language, problem solving and decision making.
An approach that explains behaviour in terms of the brain, nervous system, hormones and genes.
An approach that asks how natural selection may have shaped mental mechanisms and behaviour.
An approach that explains behaviour in terms of social relationships, cultural norms and historical context.
The comparison of psychological processes across cultures to test which findings are universal and which are culture-specific.
Psychology developed from within a particular culture, using its own concepts and values rather than imported Western frameworks.
The scientific study of strengths, well-being and the conditions that help people and communities flourish.
Research participants drawn mostly from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic societies, which limits how far findings generalise.
A discredited 19th-century practice, associated with Franz Gall, that tried to read character from bumps on the skull.
The 'spirit of the times': the intellectual and cultural climate that makes certain ideas more likely to emerge and be accepted.
Drawing on several theoretical perspectives together rather than relying on a single school of thought.
German scientist who opened an experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879, often taken as the founding of psychology as a separate science.
American philosopher-psychologist whose 1890 book The Principles of Psychology helped launch functionalism.
Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis and emphasised unconscious motives and early experience.
The first woman awarded a PhD in psychology (Cornell, 1894), known for work on animal cognition.
Pioneering memory and self researcher who completed Harvard's PhD requirements but was denied the degree because she was a woman; she later became the first female APA president.
Arab scholar (c. 965–1040) whose Book of Optics argued that vision results from light entering the eye and used systematic experiments to study perception.
The idea that mental life is built from links between ideas or events that occur together.
A systematic cycle of observing, forming hypotheses, testing them with data and revising ideas in light of the results.
A well-developed set of ideas that explains a range of observations and generates testable predictions.
A specific, testable prediction about the relationship between variables, usually derived from a theory.
The property of a claim that could, in principle, be shown false by evidence; a key criterion for scientific statements.
A precise statement of how a concept will be measured or manipulated in a particular study, such as 'anxiety = score on a given questionnaire'.
Any characteristic or condition that can take different values across people, times or situations.
The factor a researcher deliberately changes to see whether it causes an effect.
The outcome a researcher measures to see whether it is affected by the independent variable.
An uncontrolled factor that varies along with the independent variable, offering an alternative explanation for the results.
Any variable other than the independent variable that could influence the outcome and add noise if not controlled.
A study in which the researcher manipulates one or more variables and controls others, allowing conclusions about cause and effect.
Placing participants into conditions by chance so that groups are equivalent on average before the manipulation.
Selecting participants so that every member of a population has an equal chance of being included.
The entire group a researcher wants to draw conclusions about.
The subset of a population that actually takes part in a study.
Participants who do not receive the treatment of interest and serve as a baseline for comparison.
Participants who receive the treatment or manipulation being tested.
An inactive treatment made to look like the real one, used to separate genuine effects from expectations.
Improvement that results from a person's belief or expectation about a treatment rather than from the treatment itself.
A design in which participants do not know which condition they are in, but the researchers do.
A design in which neither participants nor the people collecting data know who is in which condition, reducing expectancy effects.
Subtle, often unintended ways a researcher's expectations influence participants' behaviour or the recording of data.
Cues in a study that hint at its purpose, leading participants to change their behaviour to fit what they think is expected.
A change in behaviour caused by the awareness of being observed; the original factory studies behind the name are now regarded as weak evidence.
A design in which every participant experiences all conditions, so each person acts as their own comparison.
A design in which each participant experiences only one condition, and groups are compared.
Varying the order of conditions across participants so that order effects do not systematically favour any condition.
A counterbalancing scheme in which each condition appears once in every ordinal position across a set of orders, using fewer orders than full permutation.
Changes in performance caused by the position of a condition in a sequence, such as practice, fatigue or boredom.
Improved performance on later trials or conditions simply because of familiarity with the task.
Lingering influence of an earlier condition on performance in a later one in a within-subjects design.
An experiment that crosses two or more independent variables so every combination of levels is tested.
The overall effect of one independent variable averaged across the levels of the others.
A result in which the effect of one independent variable depends on the level of another.
A study comparing groups that were not formed by random assignment, such as existing classes or genders, which weakens causal claims.
Research that measures how variables relate without manipulating them; it can show association but not establish cause.
Watching and recording behaviour in its everyday setting without intervening.
An in-depth investigation of a single person, group or event, often used for rare conditions.
A method that collects self-reported information from many people using questionnaires or interviews.
A written set of questions used to gather self-reports about attitudes, behaviours or experiences.
A design that follows the same participants over time to track change.
A design that compares different age groups or cohorts at a single point in time.
The degree to which a study rules out alternative explanations so that changes in the outcome can be attributed to the manipulation.
The degree to which findings generalise to other people, settings and times.
How closely a study's tasks and setting resemble real-life situations.
The extent to which independent observers give the same scores or codes to the same behaviour.
A small preliminary run of a study used to check procedures, timing and materials before the main data collection.
A measure confirming that the independent variable had the intended psychological effect on participants.
Principles and rules that protect the rights, dignity and welfare of participants and the integrity of research.
A 1979 U.S. report setting out three core principles for research with humans: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
A Belmont principle requiring that people be treated as autonomous agents and that those with reduced autonomy receive extra protection.
An ethical principle requiring researchers to maximise possible benefits and minimise possible harms.
A Belmont principle requiring that the burdens and benefits of research be shared fairly across groups.
A committee that reviews proposed studies to make sure participants are protected and ethical standards are met.
A participant's voluntary agreement to take part after being told the purpose, procedures, risks and their right to withdraw.
Voluntary permission given by a person who understands what they are agreeing to.
Deliberately withholding or misrepresenting information about a study; permitted only when justified, unlikely to cause harm and followed by debriefing.
Explaining a study's true purpose to participants after they take part, correcting any deception and addressing any distress.
The obligation to protect participants' information so it is not disclosed without permission.
Collecting data in a way that cannot be linked to any individual's identity.
A participant's entitlement to stop taking part at any time without penalty.
Groups such as children, prisoners or people with impaired decision-making capacity who need additional safeguards in research.
Risk of harm no greater than that encountered in daily life or routine examinations.
The American Psychological Association's Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct, which guides research, teaching and practice.
Guiding principles for animal research: Replace animals where possible, Reduce the numbers used and Refine procedures to lessen suffering.
A 1947 set of research ethics principles, written after trials of Nazi doctors, that made voluntary consent essential.
The World Medical Association's statement of ethical principles for medical research involving human participants, first adopted in 1964.
A U.S. Public Health Service study (1932–1972) in which Black men with syphilis were deceived and left untreated, prompting major ethics reforms.
Evaluation of a manuscript or proposal by independent experts before it is published or funded.
Methods for collecting, organising, summarising and drawing conclusions from numerical data.
Numbers and graphs that summarise the main features of a data set, such as averages and spread.
Recorded observations or measurements collected in a study.
A table or graph showing how often each value or range of values occurs in a data set.
A bar graph of a frequency distribution for a continuous variable, with adjacent bars for each score range.
The four levels—nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio—that determine which mathematical operations are meaningful for a variable.
A measurement level that sorts cases into named categories with no order, such as blood type.
A measurement level that ranks cases but does not guarantee equal distances between ranks, such as finishing position in a race.
A measurement level with equal distances between values but no true zero, such as temperature in Celsius.
A measurement level with equal intervals and a true zero, allowing statements like 'twice as much', such as reaction time.
The arithmetic average: the sum of scores divided by the number of scores.
The middle score when data are ordered; it is less affected by extreme values than the mean.
The most frequently occurring score in a data set.
The difference between the highest and lowest scores.
The average of the squared deviations of scores from the mean, a measure of spread.
The square root of the variance; roughly, the typical distance of scores from the mean.
The spread of the middle 50% of scores, from the 25th to the 75th percentile.
A graph showing the median, quartiles and extreme values of a distribution, useful for spotting skew and outliers.
A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution in which mean, median and mode coincide; about 68% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
The degree to which a distribution is asymmetric, with a longer tail on one side.
A distribution with a long tail toward high values; the mean is usually pulled above the median.
A distribution with a long tail toward low values; the mean is usually pulled below the median.
A distribution with two distinct peaks, often suggesting two subgroups in the data.
A description of how heavy the tails of a distribution are compared with a normal distribution.
A score that lies far from most of the other scores and may reflect error or a genuinely unusual case.
A standardised score showing how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean.
The percentage of scores in a distribution that fall at or below a given score.
A measurement problem in which a task is so hard that most scores cluster at the bottom, hiding real differences.
A measurement problem in which a task is so easy that most scores cluster at the top, hiding real differences.
A statistical relationship in which two variables tend to change together.
A number from −1 to +1 indicating the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables.
The most common correlation coefficient, measuring linear association between two interval or ratio variables.
A correlation coefficient computed on ranks, suitable for ordinal data or monotonic but non-linear relationships.
A graph plotting pairs of scores as points, used to see the form and strength of a relationship.
The square of the correlation (r²), indicating the proportion of variance in one variable shared with another.
The possibility that a correlation between two variables is produced by a separate variable that influences both.
The difficulty, in correlational data, of knowing whether A causes B or B causes A.
Perceiving a relationship between variables when none exists, often because of memorable co-occurrences.
The straight line that best predicts one variable from another by minimising squared prediction errors.
The tendency for extreme scores on one measurement to be followed by less extreme scores on the next, purely because of measurement noise.
A narrowed spread of scores in a sample that weakens the observed correlation compared with the full population.
The time between the onset of a stimulus and a participant's response, a core measure in cognitive experiments.
The body's network of nerve cells that carries and processes information.
A nerve cell specialised for receiving, integrating and transmitting electrical and chemical signals.
A non-neuronal cell that supports, insulates, nourishes and protects neurons and helps regulate their signalling.
A branching extension of a neuron that receives signals from other neurons.
The cell body of a neuron, containing the nucleus and integrating incoming signals.
The long fibre that carries an action potential away from the cell body toward other cells.
The region where the axon joins the cell body and where action potentials are usually triggered.
A fatty insulating layer formed by glial cells around many axons, which speeds signal conduction.
A small gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed and the signal is regenerated.
The rapid, jumping transmission of an action potential from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon.
The end of an axon branch that releases neurotransmitter into the synapse.
The junction where one neuron communicates with another cell, usually across a tiny gap.
The narrow space between the sending and receiving neuron at a chemical synapse.
A chemical messenger released by a neuron that crosses the synapse and binds to receptors on another cell.
A protein on a cell membrane that responds when a particular chemical, such as a neurotransmitter, binds to it.
The stable voltage difference across a neuron's membrane when it is not firing, typically around −70 millivolts.
A brief, self-propagating reversal of membrane voltage that travels down the axon.
The membrane voltage that must be reached at the axon hillock for an action potential to fire.
A shift of the membrane potential in the positive direction, making firing more likely.
A shift of the membrane potential to more negative values, making firing less likely.
The return of the membrane potential toward its resting value after depolarization, mainly through potassium outflow.
A short interval after an action potential during which the neuron cannot fire, or needs stronger stimulation to fire.
The rule that an action potential either fires fully or not at all; stimulus strength is coded by firing rate, not spike size.
A membrane protein that uses energy to move sodium ions out of and potassium ions into the cell, maintaining the resting potential.
A pore in the cell membrane that opens or closes to let specific ions pass, shaping electrical signals.
A small depolarization in the receiving neuron that makes it more likely to fire.
A small hyperpolarization in the receiving neuron that makes it less likely to fire.
The reabsorption of a neurotransmitter by the sending neuron, ending its action in the synapse.
A drug or chemical that mimics or enhances the action of a neurotransmitter.
A drug or chemical that blocks or reduces the action of a neurotransmitter.
A neurotransmitter involved in muscle activation, attention and memory.
A neurotransmitter involved in movement, motivation and reward-related learning.
A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep, appetite and many other functions.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.
The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, important for learning and memory.
A neurotransmitter and hormone involved in arousal, alertness and the stress response.
Natural opioid-like chemicals in the body that reduce pain and can produce feelings of well-being.
A 1952 mathematical model, based on squid giant-axon experiments, describing how voltage-gated sodium and potassium currents generate action potentials.
A simplified neuron model in which input charges the membrane, charge slowly leaks away, and a spike is emitted and the voltage reset when a threshold is crossed.
The idea that neurons convey stimulus intensity through how often they fire per second.
The brain and spinal cord.
The bundle of nerve tissue running through the spine that links the brain to the body and controls simple reflexes.
A fast, automatic response to a stimulus, often handled by the spinal cord without brain involvement.
All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, connecting them to the rest of the body.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary movements and carries sensory information.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion.
The branch of the autonomic system that prepares the body for action and stress.
The branch of the autonomic system that calms the body and supports rest and digestion.
A network of glands that release hormones into the bloodstream to regulate body functions.
A chemical messenger released into the bloodstream that affects target tissues elsewhere in the body.
A small gland at the base of the brain, controlled by the hypothalamus, that regulates many other endocrine glands.
Glands above the kidneys that release hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, especially during stress.
The nervous system's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience or injury.
A segment of DNA that carries instructions for building proteins and influences traits.
The passing of genetic characteristics from parents to offspring.
The study of changes in gene activity that do not alter the DNA sequence, often triggered by environmental factors.
The organ inside the skull that controls behaviour, thought, emotion and bodily functions.
The thin, folded outer layer of the brain's hemispheres, involved in perception, thought, language and voluntary action.
The front region of each hemisphere, involved in planning, decision making, movement control and speech production.
The front-most part of the frontal lobe, central to working memory, self-control and goal-directed behaviour.
A strip at the back of the frontal lobe that sends commands for voluntary movement.
The upper-rear region of each hemisphere, involved in touch, body position and spatial attention.
A strip at the front of the parietal lobe that processes touch, temperature and pain from body regions.
The region on each side of the brain involved in hearing, language comprehension and memory.
The rear region of the brain, specialised for processing vision.
A region usually in the left frontal lobe whose damage impairs speech production while comprehension is relatively spared.
A region usually in the left temporal lobe whose damage impairs language comprehension, producing fluent but meaningless speech.
The thick band of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
A condition in which the corpus callosum has been cut, usually to treat severe epilepsy, so the hemispheres can be tested separately.
The tendency for certain functions, such as language, to rely more on one hemisphere than the other.
A set of interconnected structures, including the hippocampus and amygdala, linked to emotion, motivation and memory.
A curved structure in the temporal lobe that is crucial for forming new long-term explicit memories and for spatial navigation.
An almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe involved in detecting threats and in emotional learning, especially fear.
A small structure below the thalamus that regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature, hormones and daily rhythms.
A central relay station that routes most incoming sensory information to the cortex.
The 'little brain' at the back of the skull that coordinates movement, balance and timing, and contributes to some learning.
The lower part of the brain, connecting to the spinal cord and controlling basic life functions such as breathing.
The lowest part of the brainstem, controlling heartbeat and breathing.
A brainstem structure that relays signals and contributes to sleep and arousal regulation.
A network of neurons in the brainstem that helps regulate arousal, alertness and sleep–wake transitions.
A group of deep brain structures involved in initiating movement and in habit and reward learning.
A 19th-century railway worker whose personality reportedly changed after an iron rod damaged his frontal lobe, an early clue to frontal-lobe functions.
Research that infers a brain area's function from the deficits that follow its damage.
Recording the brain's electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp, giving excellent timing but coarse location.
An EEG waveform time-locked to a specific stimulus or response, obtained by averaging many trials.
A brain-imaging method that tracks changes in blood oxygenation as an indirect measure of neural activity.
An imaging technique that tracks a radioactive tracer to measure brain metabolism or neurotransmitter activity.
A technique that uses magnetic pulses through the scalp to briefly excite or disrupt activity in a cortical area.
Awareness of oneself and one's surroundings, including thoughts, sensations and feelings.
A roughly 24-hour cycle in physiology and behaviour, such as the sleep–wake cycle.
A cluster of cells in the hypothalamus that acts as the body's master clock, synchronised mainly by light.
A hormone released by the pineal gland, mainly in darkness, that signals night-time to the body and promotes sleep.
A naturally recurring, reversible state of reduced awareness and responsiveness with characteristic brain-wave stages.
Non-rapid eye movement sleep, made up of stages N1 to N3 and progressing from light to deep sleep.
A sleep stage with rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, a wake-like EEG and near-paralysis of skeletal muscles.
The deepest NREM stage (N3), dominated by large, slow delta waves.
High-amplitude, low-frequency brain waves (below about 4 Hz) typical of deep sleep.
Brain waves of roughly 8–12 Hz seen when a person is awake but relaxed, often with eyes closed.
A brief burst of rhythmic brain activity at about 11–16 Hz, characteristic of stage N2 sleep and linked to memory consolidation.
A single large, sharp negative-then-positive EEG wave that appears during stage N2 sleep, sometimes in response to sounds.
A graph that plots the sequence of sleep stages across a night, showing cycles of NREM and REM sleep.
A sleep study that records brain waves, eye movements, muscle tone, breathing and heart rate overnight.
Persistent difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, causing daytime impairment.
A disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops or becomes very shallow during sleep, fragmenting rest.
A neurological disorder marked by overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden intrusions of REM sleep, sometimes with loss of muscle tone.
A state of insufficient sleep that impairs attention, mood, memory and health.
A sequence of images, feelings and thoughts experienced during sleep, most vivid in REM sleep.
The proposal that dreams arise when the brain tries to make sense of random brainstem activity during REM sleep.
A state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility induced by a set of instructions.
Practices that train attention and awareness, often to achieve calm or mental clarity.
A substance that alters perception, mood, thought or consciousness by acting on the nervous system.
The need for increasing amounts of a drug to achieve the same effect after repeated use.
Unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that occur when a person stops using a drug they depend on.
A drug, such as caffeine or amphetamine, that increases nervous-system activity and alertness.
A drug, such as alcohol, that slows nervous-system activity.
A drug that distorts perception and can cause sensory experiences without external stimuli.
A class of drugs, including morphine and heroin, that act on opioid receptors to relieve pain and can produce dependence.
The detection of physical energy by sense organs and its conversion into neural signals.
The brain's organisation and interpretation of sensory information into meaningful experience.
The conversion of physical energy, such as light or sound, into neural signals by sensory receptors.
The study of quantitative relationships between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.
The weakest stimulus intensity a person can detect on a set proportion of trials, conventionally half.
The smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect on a set proportion of trials; also called the just-noticeable difference.
The minimum change in stimulus intensity needed for a person to notice a difference.
The principle that the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity.
The constant ratio ΔI/I in Weber's law, which differs across senses and indicates how sensitive a sense is to change.
The proposal that perceived magnitude grows with the logarithm of physical intensity.
The finding that perceived magnitude equals physical intensity raised to a power, with the exponent varying by sense.
A psychophysical method in which a fixed set of intensities is presented many times in random order to estimate a threshold.
A psychophysical method in which intensity is raised or lowered in steps until the participant's response changes.
A psychophysical method in which the participant adjusts a stimulus until it just becomes detectable or matches a standard.
An adaptive method that makes the stimulus harder after correct responses and easier after errors, homing in on a threshold.
A curve relating stimulus intensity to the proportion of 'detected' or correct responses.
A framework that separates a person's sensitivity to a signal from their bias toward saying 'yes' or 'no'.
In signal detection, correctly reporting a signal that was present.
In signal detection, reporting a signal when none was present.
In signal detection, failing to report a signal that was present.
In signal detection, correctly reporting that no signal was present.
A signal detection measure of sensitivity, computed as the z-score of the hit rate minus the z-score of the false-alarm rate.
A signal detection measure of response bias; a positive value means a conservative tendency to say 'no', a negative value a liberal tendency to say 'yes'.
A receiver operating characteristic plot of hit rate against false-alarm rate across criteria; curves bowing further toward the top-left show greater sensitivity.
A decrease in sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus over time.
Perception driven by the features of incoming sensory data.
Perception guided by expectations, knowledge and context.
A readiness to perceive something in a particular way because of expectations or recent experience.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing rods and cones.
Retinal receptors that work in dim light and support black-and-white and peripheral vision.
Retinal receptors concentrated in the fovea that work in bright light and support colour and fine detail.
The small central pit of the retina packed with cones, giving the sharpest vision.
The place where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no receptors, so light falling there is not detected.
The sense of sight, based on detecting light with the eyes.
The sense that detects sound waves, transduced by hair cells in the cochlea.
The theory that colour vision depends on three types of cones most sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths.
The theory that colour is coded in opposing pairs—red–green, blue–yellow and black–white—explaining afterimages.
Neurons in the visual cortex that respond selectively to specific features such as edges, angles or motion.
The fluid-filled, coiled structure in the inner ear where sound vibrations are converted into neural signals.
The theory that pitch is coded by where along the cochlea's basilar membrane vibration is greatest.
The theory that pitch is coded by the rate at which auditory neurons fire.
The theory that signals in the spinal cord can open or close a 'gate' that modulates how much pain reaches the brain.
An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or possible tissue damage.
The sense of the position and movement of one's own body parts.
The sense of balance and head movement, based in the inner ear.
The sense of smell.
The sense of taste.
The skin sense that detects pressure, vibration and texture.
Rules describing how the visual system groups elements into wholes, such as proximity, similarity, closure and continuity.
The perceptual separation of a scene into an object (figure) that stands out from its surroundings (ground).
The Gestalt tendency to group elements that are close together.
The Gestalt tendency to group elements that look alike.
The Gestalt tendency to fill in gaps and see incomplete figures as whole.
The ability to see the world in three dimensions and judge distance.
The slight difference between the images in the two eyes, used by the brain to judge depth.
Depth cues available to a single eye, such as relative size, interposition, texture gradient and linear perspective.
A depth cue in which parallel lines appear to converge with distance.
Perceiving objects as stable in size, shape and colour despite changes in the image on the retina.
Perceiving an object as the same size even when its retinal image shrinks or grows with distance.
A visual stimulus that is systematically perceived differently from its physical properties.
A distorted, trapezoidal room that looks rectangular from one viewpoint, so people in different corners appear to differ dramatically in size.
An illusion in which two identical horizontal lines placed between converging lines look different in length, the one nearer the convergence appearing longer.
An illusion in which a line ending in outward-pointing fins looks longer than an identical line ending in inward-pointing arrowheads.
An illusion in which seeing lips form one syllable while hearing another produces the perception of a third, blended syllable.
A visually distinguishable mouth shape associated with one or more speech sounds; several phonemes can share the same viseme.
The brain's combination of information from different senses into a single, coherent percept.
The set of processes that select some information for further processing while other information is ignored.
Focusing on one source of information while filtering out others.
Attempting to attend to two or more tasks or sources at the same time.
Maintaining focus on a task over an extended period; also called vigilance.
The decline in detection performance that occurs over time in long, monotonous monitoring tasks.
A procedure in which different messages are played to each ear and the participant attends to one of them.
Repeating aloud an attended message as it is heard, used in dichotic listening to keep attention on one ear.
The ability to focus on one conversation in a noisy setting while still noticing personally significant information, such as one's own name, elsewhere.
Broadbent's early-selection model, in which unattended inputs are blocked on the basis of physical features before their meaning is analysed.
Treisman's model in which unattended messages are weakened rather than fully blocked, so important words can still break through.
The view that all inputs are analysed for meaning and selection happens only before responding or entering awareness.
Lavie's theory that distractors are processed less when the main task demands heavy perceptual load.
Failing to notice a fully visible but unexpected object or event because attention is engaged elsewhere, as in the 'invisible gorilla' study.
Failing to notice large changes in a scene, especially when the change coincides with a brief interruption.
A brief period, roughly 200–500 ms after spotting a first target in a rapid stream, during which a second target is often missed.
A method in which items are flashed one after another at the same location at high speed.
A task in which a person looks for a target among distractors; response time is measured as the number of items changes.
A visual search in which the target differs by a single feature and 'pops out', so search time barely depends on the number of items.
A visual search in which the target is defined by a combination of features, so search time typically rises with the number of items.
Treisman's theory that basic features are registered in parallel but attention is needed to bind them into objects.
A mistaken combination of features from different objects, such as seeing a red X when a red O and a blue X were shown.
A paradigm in which a cue directs attention to a location; responses are faster for targets at cued (valid) than uncued (invalid) locations.
Attention captured automatically by a sudden or salient external event.
Attention directed voluntarily according to goals or instructions.
Slower responses to a location that was cued a few hundred milliseconds earlier, which may encourage search of new locations.
The involuntary drawing of attention by a stimulus that is not relevant to the current goal.
Slower and more error-prone naming of an ink colour when the printed word names a different colour.
A task in which people respond to a central target while ignoring flanking items; incongruent flankers slow responses.
Faster responses when the response side matches the stimulus location, even when location is irrelevant to the task.
Alternating between tasks; responses are usually slower on switch trials than on repeat trials, a difference called the switch cost.
A drop in performance when two tasks are done at the same time, compared with doing each alone.
The delay in responding to a second stimulus when it follows closely after a first stimulus that also requires a response.
Processing that occurs quickly, effortlessly and without conscious control, often after extensive practice.
The tendency for faster responses to be less accurate, and more accurate responses to be slower.
The finding that choice reaction time increases linearly with the information in the stimulus set, i.e. with the logarithm of the number of equally likely alternatives.
A model predicting that the time to move to a target increases with the logarithm of the ratio of distance to target width.
A model of reaction-time distributions formed by combining a normal and an exponential component, with parameters μ, σ and τ, where τ captures the slow tail.
Shifts of attention away from the current task toward unrelated thoughts.
A relatively lasting change in behaviour or knowledge that results from experience.
A decrease in response to a stimulus that is repeated without consequence.
An increase in response to a stimulus after exposure to a strong or noxious stimulus.
Learning in which a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response after being paired with a stimulus that naturally produces that response.
A stimulus that naturally triggers a response without prior learning, such as food producing salivation.
An unlearned, automatic response to an unconditioned stimulus.
A formerly neutral stimulus that triggers a response after being paired with an unconditioned stimulus.
A learned response to a conditioned stimulus.
The initial stage of learning, when a response is being established.
The weakening of a learned response when the conditioned stimulus is no longer followed by the unconditioned stimulus, or a behaviour is no longer reinforced.
The reappearance of an extinguished response after a rest period.
Responding to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus.
Learning to respond to one stimulus but not to similar ones.
Using an established conditioned stimulus to condition a new neutral stimulus.
A learned avoidance of a food after it is followed by illness, which can form after a single pairing and a long delay.
An inborn readiness to learn certain associations, such as fear of snakes or taste–illness links, more easily than others.

Increasing a behaviour by removing an unpleasant stimulus after it.
Any consequence that decreases the likelihood of the behaviour it follows.
Decreasing a behaviour by adding an unpleasant stimulus after it.
Decreasing a behaviour by removing a pleasant stimulus after it.

A consequence that becomes rewarding through association with primary reinforcers, such as money or praise.

Reinforcement delivered after an unpredictable number of responses, producing high, steady response rates.

A mnemonic in which items are mentally placed at locations along a familiar route and later recalled by mentally walking the route.

Identifying previously learned information when it is presented again, as in multiple-choice questions.
Learning material again that was previously learned; faster relearning (savings) shows some memory remained.

The loss or inaccessibility of previously stored information.
Disruption of new learning by older memories.
Disruption of older memories by new learning.
Forgetting attributed to the fading of memory traces over time.

Loss of memory for events that occurred before the onset of amnesia.

The process by which new memories become stabilised over time.
The re-stabilisation of a memory after it has been retrieved, during which it may be modified.

Representing sensory experiences in the mind without the corresponding stimulus.

Ignoring how common something is in the population when estimating probability.

A newborn's tendency to turn toward a touch on the cheek and open the mouth.

Vygotsky's term for the range of tasks a learner can do with guidance but not yet alone.

A test, such as the Sally–Anne task, of whether a child understands that someone can hold a belief that is mistaken.
The repetitive consonant–vowel sounds infants produce at around six months, before first words.
Early two-word utterances that contain mainly content words, such as 'want milk'.
A deep, enduring emotional bond between a child and a caregiver.

Fear of unfamiliar people that commonly appears in the second half of the first year.
A person's characteristic emotional reactivity and intensity, visible from infancy.

Changes in reasoning about right and wrong; Kohlberg described preconventional, conventional and postconventional levels.
The period of life between infancy and adolescence.
The transition period from childhood to adulthood.
The period of sexual maturation during which a person becomes capable of reproduction.

A decline in memory and other thinking abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

The desire to do something because it is interesting or satisfying in itself.

A complex, unlearned behaviour pattern found throughout a species.

An emotion associated with loss or disappointment.

The ability to adapt well and recover in the face of adversity.
A person's own evaluation of their life satisfaction and their balance of positive and negative emotions.
A state of deep, effortless absorption in a challenging activity that matches one's skills.

A person's characteristic and relatively enduring patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving.

A mood-stabilising medication used to treat bipolar disorder.
A treatment for severe depression in which a brief electrical current induces a controlled seizure under anaesthesia.
The movement of people with serious mental illness out of large psychiatric hospitals into community care.
Ways that cultural groups experience, understand and communicate suffering or problematic behaviour.
A practitioner's awareness, knowledge and skills for working effectively with clients from diverse backgrounds.
Methods for drawing conclusions about populations from sample data while quantifying uncertainty.
The default assumption that there is no effect or no difference in the population.
The hypothesis that there is an effect or difference in the population.
The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true.
A result whose p-value falls below a chosen alpha level, conventionally .05.
The threshold probability chosen in advance for rejecting the null hypothesis; it equals the Type I error rate when the null is true.
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true; a false positive.
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false; a false negative.
The probability that a test will detect an effect of a given size if it truly exists; equal to one minus the Type II error rate.
A calculation used to determine the sample size needed to detect an expected effect with a desired level of power.
A measure of the magnitude of an effect, independent of sample size.
An effect size equal to the difference between two means divided by their pooled standard deviation; Cohen suggested 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 as rough benchmarks for small, medium and large.
An ANOVA effect size showing the proportion of variance associated with a factor after excluding other factors.
A range of values, computed from sample data by a procedure that captures the true population value in a stated proportion (such as 95%) of repeated samples.
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution; it shows how much a statistic such as the mean would vary across samples.
The distribution of a statistic across many possible samples of the same size.
The principle that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, whatever the population's shape.
The number of values free to vary when estimating a statistic, used to choose the correct reference distribution.
A test comparing two means, such as two groups or two conditions, relative to their variability.
A t-test comparing two measurements from the same participants.
A test comparing means across three or more groups or conditions by partitioning variance.
In ANOVA, the ratio of variance between groups to variance within groups.
A test of whether observed category frequencies differ from expected frequencies.
A technique that predicts an outcome from several predictor variables at once.
A regression model that includes both fixed effects and random effects, such as variation across participants and items.
The rise in the chance of at least one false positive when many statistical tests are run.
An adjustment that divides the alpha level by the number of tests to control the overall false-positive rate.
A procedure for testing whether an effect is small enough to be considered practically zero.
An approach that updates the probability of hypotheses in light of data, combining prior beliefs with evidence.
The ratio of how well two competing hypotheses predict the observed data.
A statistical method combining the results of many studies to estimate an overall effect size.
The tendency for studies with significant or striking results to be published more often than those with null results.
The concern that unpublished null results sitting in researchers' files distort the published literature.
A scatterplot of study effect sizes against their precision, used to look for signs of publication bias.
Repeating a study to see whether its findings hold.
Repeating a study as closely as possible to the original methods.
Testing the same hypothesis with different methods or measures.
The realisation, especially in the 2010s, that many published findings in psychology and other fields did not hold up when repeated.
A 2015 collaborative effort that repeated 100 published psychology studies and found that fewer than half produced statistically significant results again.
A series of large collaborative projects in which many laboratories run the same studies to test replicability and variation across sites.
The claim that self-control draws on a limited resource that is used up by effort; a large multi-lab replication found an effect close to zero.
Methods choices, such as selective reporting or flexible stopping rules, that inflate false-positive findings without being outright fraud.
The many analytic decisions researchers can make, which can be exploited, knowingly or not, to produce significant results.
Trying different analyses, exclusions or stopping points until a significant p-value appears, then reporting only that result.
Hypothesising After the Results are Known: presenting an explanation formed after seeing data as if it had been predicted in advance.
Recording hypotheses, methods and analysis plans in a time-stamped public registry before collecting or analysing data.
A publication format in which the introduction and methods are peer-reviewed before data collection, and the journal commits to publish regardless of the results.
Practices that make research transparent and accessible, such as sharing data, materials, code and preprints.
Making a study's raw data publicly available so others can check and reuse it.
A free online platform for preregistering studies and sharing project materials, data and code.
A version of a research paper shared publicly before formal peer review.
Obtaining the same results when the original data are reanalysed with the same methods.
Fabrication, falsification or plagiarism in proposing, performing or reporting research.
The writing and formatting conventions of the American Psychological Association for scientific reports.
A brief summary at the start of a research report describing its purpose, method, results and conclusions.
A summary and synthesis of existing research on a topic.
Systematic investigation aimed at producing reliable knowledge.
A number from 0 to 1 expressing how likely an event is.
Systematically watching and recording behaviour or events.
A method of gathering information through direct conversation with a participant.
